operations.evidence: for covered crimes and populations CSEW is a better long-term trend indicator than police recorded crime; it is unaffected by changes in police counting rules; it is also unaffected by changes in reporting and recording practice
the statement does not apply to crimes outside CSEW coverage; questionnaire changes still require measure-version checks
the main CSEW estimate excludes homicide; it excludes crimes against businesses and drug possession; sexual offences are excluded from the main face-to-face crime estimate
excluded crimes must not be represented as zero; other sources or separate modules are required

people aged 16 or over complete a separate tablet module on domestic and sexual violence; these results are reported separately; the module reduces pressure to disclose sensitive experiences to an interviewer
self-completion outputs have separate definitions and bases; they must not be silently merged into headline crime
fraud and computer-misuse questions were added in October 2015; sufficient data were available for first publication in July 2016; the estimates entered headline crime after a full interview year
pre-2015 headline series did not include these questions; series comparisons require the fraud-coverage boundary

fraud and computer-misuse questions initially went to half the sample; from October 2017 they were asked of the full sample; the staged design protected the historical survey series while testing burden
half-sample and full-sample periods need design metadata; sample expansion is not an incident-date change
some respondents may say they reported a crime to police when they did not; ONS identifies this as a socially desirable response risk; the issue is a non-sampling error
self-reported police contact is not administrative proof; the direction and size of bias may vary
some incidents can be miscoded during interview or coding; specially trained coders assign offence codes; coding quality is a separate uncertainty source from sampling error
a coded survey offence is not a police-recorded offence; miscoding risk must not be ignored in small differences
police recorded crime is produced from a live administrative system; records can change as investigations proceed; offence categories can change, for example from theft to robbery
published snapshots are not immutable event logs; later classifications can supersede earlier ones
forces send provisional figures to the Home Office monthly; returns include revised totals for previously supplied months; Home Office validation can prompt resubmission
monthly values must be versioned; a revised month must not be counted as an additional month
every three months the Home Office takes a database snapshot; forces receive counts for the last eight quarters to quality assure; historical counts can be updated during this process
snapshot QA does not create an immutable historical series; the snapshot date must accompany extracted values
figures for the same period may differ between publications; differences reflect subsequent force revisions; ONS states revisions tend to be small
small revisions are not zero revisions; values must be tied to publication edition
quarterly data tables include differences between current and preceding publications; the table supports revision transparency; revisions are part of the official release process
a difference table is not a replacement for the current data table; revision direction must not be inferred without values
Crime in England and Wales is published quarterly; publication is approximately 14 weeks after quarter end; timeliness is distinct from punctuality
the lag is approximate rather than guaranteed; publication lag is not incident-to-police lag

HOCR and NCRS implementation prevents direct comparison of police recorded crime before YE March 2003; the boundary affects long-term police series; HMICFRS inspections provide force-variation context
pre-2003 figures are not invalid but require separate methodology; the boundary does not apply identically to CSEW

a comparable subset was constructed for offences covered by both measures; more than three-quarters of recent CSEW offences fall into comparable categories; the subset supports adjusted comparison between sources
the subset is not the full CSEW or full police series; comparison requires the official mapping
CSEW offence coding is designed to align closely with police-recorded definitions; alignment supports source comparison; the two sources still use different collection methods
close alignment is not identity; changes to either coding system require version checks
ONS crime statistics are released as aggregate data; they are publicly available free of charge; publication uses the Open Government Licence
aggregate release does not provide confidential record-level data; licensing does not remove statistical limitations
publication dates are pre-announced; ONS states at least six to eight weeks of notice; the calendar covers planned release timing
pre-announcement is not a guarantee against justified changes; release date differs from reference period
the Home Office supplies ONS with a document describing checks and QA for quarterly delivery; the document uses an agreed template; the handoff records the validation performed before ONS compilation
the QA document is not an independent external audit; its scope must be matched to the delivered edition
the Home Office must communicate corrections made after data delivery; ONS states this applies regardless of how minor the correction is; the process supports publication revision control
notification does not mean every prior publication changes materially; minor and major corrections must remain distinguishable
Home Office analysts quality-assure the draft bulletin; ONS considers their comments; final editorial responsibility remains with ONS
subject-matter review does not transfer editorial ownership; editorial responsibility is separate from source-data ownership
the responsible statistician signs off the final draft before publication; sign-off follows compilation and quality assurance; the control is part of the official publication process
sign-off does not make administrative data error-free; later corrections can still be issued

crime-data quality is influenced by different IT systems and software versions across forces; some forces can change their systems directly while others depend on suppliers; supplier-dependent changes can be slower and more costly
system variation must not be converted directly into force performance rankings; the finding is contextual rather than parcel-level

the 2023 Counting Rules review introduced a single principal crime rule for most offences; modern slavery and passport-application fraud remain exceptions; OSR noted concerns about effects on understanding domestic-abuse offending patterns
the rule change can create classification discontinuities; the exceptions and domestic-abuse caveat must remain explicit

Official source rows 611-630 were published in two bounded files with revision, comparability, governance and OSR system-variation controls.
Operation rows 1371-1474 preserve separate validation and limitation entries for website line-by-line visibility.

All 12 candidates remain unjoined at confidence zero; source rows 581-630 and operation rows 1371-1474 were published without a second runner, task, candidate value, business row, database write, migration or deployment.
